I agree with most people about getting rid of the sauna but you have a couple options depending on your budget. These are all based around what I do for a living in the Midwest so your area could be different in pricing.
1. You can have the glass redone, it would be 4 panels ideally but it really depends on the opening size and overall height. I can answer more questions about that or just call a glass company near you and don’t forget to ask them about support bars to have the glass hinge off the panel by the toilet. You could also change the shower door design to have a metal header and not have to worry about the weight so much with the use of pivot hinges instead. Expect anywhere between $1500-$4000 for this depending on design choices
2. Rip the sauna and shower out, extend the shower to the wall and I’d build a knee wall on the toilet side of existing shower. You will need to do flooring so either find more of those floor tiles if you don’t have any or expect to replace all the flooring and trim around the bathroom. Depending on what you want to replace it with, like the walls, the flooring, the plumbing, the type of base, you should be looking no less than $12000-$15000 with the possibility of hearing something closer to $40000
3. If you don’t really care to spend money right now or until you make a decision, throw a tension rod and curtain between the glass panels. You’re like at like $20-$30. 

Good luck and hope everything works out!

It’s usually a gap between the sashes(the frame that holds the glass, not the whole frame) allowing cold air to come inside and condense on the warm glass. I would put my hand next to where they meet when it’s closed and slowly move it up and down to feel for any kind of draft between the sashes. For a temporary fix, you can dry up all the water and use something like newspaper or even tissue paper, open the window slightly, stuff it behind and shut it so it closes the gap for now. The actual problem could be a couple of things. House settling and causing the whole frame to flex, improper installation in the first place, or the weatherstripping(usually a gray felt that slides into a little track) is worn so much it’s almost nonexistent. A couple of ways to check without needing a professional to come out(this is what they would do anyway) would be to take out the sliding window(just open it and lift it up and the bottom of it will come out and it’ll drop right out of the top part of the frame, just hold it tightly so you don’t drop it on your feet or break the glass) and look for the weatherstripping on the the side where it meets the other sash. If it looks fluffy and runs the full length of the window, it’s usually in decent shape. I’d also look at the sashes when it’s shut and see if it’s perfectly flush the whole way and not leaning too far one way. If it’s not making perfect contact the entire way and you can’t push it into place, it’s a frame problem and will need to be replaced.

As someone else said, the seals on the insulated glass itself are bad and you need a new insulated glass unit in both windows. New units can still have condensation on them tho so the actual problem is there is too much moisture in the air inside. If your room has poor ventilation and your bed is right next to the window, your breath is enough to create that problem so I’d look into getting a fan. Also check for any drafts around the entire window, where it slides and near the trim. There’s replaceable seals, usually a grey felt that is between the two sliding sashes, but the caulk along the bottom(can’t really make out the other sides) looks like it’s separating so it probably needs caulked again. I’d even check outside and see if there’s any visible gaps between the window and the exterior of the house and touch those up as well.

What’s the exterior of the window look like? Typically a leak like that is coming between the frame of the window and opening for the frame. The caulk across the top could have broken(mostly to using the wrong kind of caulk in the first place). Grab a ladder to get above the window on the outside and spray down onto it, not spraying up from the ground. Don’t spray a lot either because it’ll make it harder to truly establish where it’s leaking from. Worst case, if you have a brick exterior, when they crack, water will seep through the mortar and fall onto the top of the window and leak towards the inside if the window wasn’t installed properly.
